charter.mission: We keep the release train running and decide what 9.x is, so that every package team can ship without negotiating a date with every other package team.
charter.process: Scope proposals come in from the package teams and from the forum. We publish the 9.x scope once, cut a release on a fixed cadence, and hold a weekly maintainers call where anything that changes another package's public API is argued and decided there rather than in a pull request thread. A breaking change ships only with a migration note and a deprecation that has already been through a release.

charter.mission: We are the engine everything else is built on: if a scene renders at all, it renders through us.
charter.process: Feature requests arrive from the package teams and bug reports arrive already labelled and routed from triage. We work against the visual test suite — a change that moves a reference image does not merge until the diff is explained — and we land WebGL and WebGPU behind one public API so no caller has to know which backend is under it.
owns: the material and mesh base classes

charter.mission: We make sure an asset that leaves any authoring tool arrives in a Babylon scene looking the way its author meant it to.
charter.process: New extensions come from the Khronos registry and broken-asset reports come from triage. Every extension lands with a sample asset in the conformance suite and a reference render; export is tested by round-tripping the same asset back out and comparing it against that render. An asset we cannot load is a bug against us even when the exporter that wrote it is the thing that is wrong.
owns: the OBJ, STL and SPLAT loaders

charter.mission: We give a scene its look: the shading, the textures and the post-processing that turn correct geometry into something worth showing.
charter.process: We build on core's material base classes rather than beside them. Every material and post-process in the library ships with a Playground that demonstrates it and a reference image in the visual suite, and anything that moves that image is reverted before the release rather than explained after it.

charter.mission: We are how a scene talks back to the person looking at it, in 2D over the canvas and in 3D inside it.
charter.process: Control requests come from the viewer, the editors and the forum, routed to us by triage. We keep the control set small and composable, ship each control in both the 2D and the 3D flavour where that makes sense, and hold the GUI editor to one rule: anything you can build by hand you can build in the editor, and it serializes to the same file either way.

charter.mission: We let someone build a material, a geometry, a particle system or a render graph by wiring boxes together, so that writing shader code stops being the price of entry.
charter.process: New blocks follow new core and materials features by one release: they land the capability, we expose it as a block with a live preview and a saved snippet. The four editors share one graph canvas and one serialization layer, so a fix to the canvas lands in all of them at once and a graph saved by one of them is readable by the others.

charter.mission: We make a running scene legible: what is in it, what it is doing, and which property is the one that is wrong.
charter.process: We follow the core API — a new property that is not in the inspector is a bug against us, not against core. Inspector v2 is built on the shared UI component library and lands feature by feature alongside v1 until it can replace it; we do not ship a v2 that can do less than the v1 it replaces.
owns: the scene explorer and the property grid

charter.mission: We are where every bug is reproduced and every feature is learned: a scene anyone can open, edit and share by link in under ten seconds.
charter.process: Every release becomes a selectable version in the playground on the day it is tagged. Snippets are immutable once saved and are never collected, because a five-year-old forum post linking to one is the documentation for that answer. The sandbox does the same job for a file someone drags in rather than code they type.

charter.mission: We make putting a 3D model on a web page a one-line job for someone who has never heard of a scene graph.
charter.process: We wrap the engine in a web component with a declarative configuration and no required JavaScript. Every configurator option maps to an attribute and every attribute is documented, and we hold the whole bundle to a size budget, because the people who use us are putting it on a product page that has a budget of its own.

charter.mission: We make real-time video and image effects composable, so an effect chain is something you assemble rather than something you write.
charter.process: Filters are authored as blocks in the smart filter editor and compiled down to one optimised shader per chain. We take the node editors' canvas as given and contribute back to it rather than forking it, and every block ships with a demo chain that runs against a live camera feed so a regression is visible rather than reported.

charter.mission: We run the same scene, unchanged, outside a browser — in a native app, on a phone, and under React Native.
charter.process: We track core's releases rather than its main branch, and our bar is parity: a Playground that works on the web should work on Native with the same output. Where a platform genuinely cannot do something we say so in the parity table, with a date or a reason, instead of quietly diverging and letting someone find out at ship time.

charter.mission: We make the engine and its editors drivable by an agent, so that “build me a scene that does this” is something a model can do rather than describe.
charter.process: Each server wraps one surface — the engine core, the node material editor, the GUI editor, the playground — and exposes it as tools with schemas an agent can read without a tutorial. We test against a suite of prompts that must each produce a scene that renders, and a tool a model consistently calls wrong is a tool we named badly rather than a model that needs a longer prompt.

charter.mission: We make a release a non-event: the build is boring, the tests are trustworthy, and tagging a version is the least interesting thing that happens that week.
charter.process: Every pull request runs the unit tests, the visual test suite and the memory-leak suite. A flaky test is quarantined the day it is noticed and then fixed or deleted inside the release — we do not carry a suite people have learned to ignore. Releases go out of CI on a tag, never off a laptop.

charter.mission: We make sure the answer to a question is on the documentation site before it is asked on the forum for the third time.
charter.process: We follow the release: every public API that ships gets a reference entry generated from its source comments, and every feature that ships with a Playground gets that Playground embedded in a page. Forum questions that keep coming back become tutorials, and a tutorial that stops running against the current release is fixed or deleted rather than left up.

charter.mission: We make sure every report reaches the team that can act on it, with a reproduction attached, before it goes stale.
charter.process: Every new issue and every forum bug report, within one working day: reproduce it in a Playground or ask for one; label it by area and severity; close duplicates with a link to the original; assign it to the owning team. Every Monday: rank the open, unassigned issues by how many users are affected and post the top ten. We do not fix bugs; we make them fixable.
owns: the label set and what each label means
